title: Freelance Time Tracking Kit
description: Track your hours in a spreadsheet, see your real hourly rate, and turn a month of logged time into a clear invoice. Timesheet with a sample week, weekly summary, fixed-price budget tracker, setup formulas and a 15-minute Friday review. Works in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Time Tracking Kit

A simple, spreadsheet-based system for tracking your working hours, turning them into accurate invoices, and seeing where your week actually goes. No app, no subscription, no account. It works in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers or LibreOffice.

## Who this is for
- Freelancers who bill by the hour and want invoices that match the work.
- Freelancers who bill by the project and want to know whether a fixed price was really worth it.
- Anyone who ends the week busy but unsure where the time went.

## What's inside
| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `timesheet.csv` | Your daily log. One row per block of work. Filled with a sample week so you can see how it works. |
| `weekly-summary.csv` | A one-row-per-week roll-up: billable hours, non-billable hours, utilisation and effective rate. |
| `project-budget-tracker.csv` | Hours budgeted vs hours used for each fixed-price project, with a warning column. |
| `setup-guide.md` | How to set up the sheets in 10 minutes, with the exact formulas to paste in. |
| `logging-habits.md` | How to log time without it taking over your day: three methods, rounding rules and category list. |
| `weekly-review.md` | A 15-minute Friday review checklist and reflection prompts. |
| `timesheet-to-invoice.md` | Step-by-step: turning a month of logged time into a clean invoice line by line, with a worked example. |

## Quick start (10 minutes)
1. Import `timesheet.csv` into your spreadsheet app (File > Import, or just open it).
2. Delete the sample rows once you've looked at them, but keep the header row.
3. Follow `setup-guide.md` to add the three formulas (hours, amount, week number).
4. Log today's work using one of the methods in `logging-habits.md`.
5. On Friday, run through `weekly-review.md` and add one row to `weekly-summary.csv`.

## The sample data
The sample week belongs to a fictional freelance designer, "Sam", billing $60/hour to two clients and running one fixed-price website project. The numbers are made up for illustration and are consistent across every file, so you can follow one week from timesheet to summary to invoice.

## Notes
- Hours are stored as decimals (1.5 = one hour thirty minutes). `setup-guide.md` explains how to convert.
- Currency is shown in dollars but nothing depends on it; use any currency.
- This kit is an organisational tool, not tax or accounting advice.

files.setup-guide.md:
# Setup guide

This takes about ten minutes. The instructions use Google Sheets / Excel formula syntax; Numbers and LibreOffice accept the same formulas.

## 1. Import the timesheet
Open `timesheet.csv` in your spreadsheet app. You should see these columns:

| Column | Letter | What goes in it |
|---|---|---|
| date | A | The day, as YYYY-MM-DD |
| week | B | Week number (formula below) |
| client | C | Client name, spelled the same way every time |
| project | D | Project name |
| task | E | Short description a client could read |
| category | F | One of the categories in `logging-habits.md` |
| billable | G | `yes`, `no` or `fixed` |
| start | H | Start time, 24-hour (09:00) |
| end | I | End time, 24-hour (11:30) |
| hours | J | Decimal hours (formula below) |
| rate | K | Hourly rate for billable rows; 0 otherwise |
| amount | L | hours x rate (formula below) |
| notes | M | Anything you'll want to remember at invoice time |

Tip: freeze the header row (View > Freeze > 1 row) so it stays visible.

## 2. Add the formulas
Put these in row 2 and fill them down. In the sample file the values are already typed in, so overwrite them with formulas once you start your own log.

**Hours (column J)** - works out the length of each block from start and end times:
```
=ROUND((I2-H2)*24*4,0)/4
```
This rounds to the nearest quarter hour. If you'd rather round to six minutes (0.1 hour), use `=ROUND((I2-H2)*24,1)`.

If your times are imported as text and the formula shows an error, use:
```
=ROUND((TIMEVALUE(I2)-TIMEVALUE(H2))*24*4,0)/4
```

**Amount (column L):**
```
=IF(G2="yes",J2*K2,0)
```

**Week number (column B):**
```
=ISOWEEKNUM(A2)
```

## 3. Converting minutes to decimal hours
If you log minutes instead of times, divide by 60:

| Minutes | Decimal hours |
|---|---|
| 15 | 0.25 |
| 20 | 0.33 |
| 30 | 0.5 |
| 45 | 0.75 |
| 50 | 0.83 |
| 90 | 1.5 |

## 4. Weekly totals
On a second tab, or below your log, add these. Change `45` to the week you're reviewing (or point it at a cell).

| Total | Formula |
|---|---|
| Billable hours | `=SUMIFS(J:J,B:B,45,G:G,"yes")` |
| Fixed-price hours | `=SUMIFS(J:J,B:B,45,G:G,"fixed")` |
| Non-billable hours | `=SUMIFS(J:J,B:B,45,G:G,"no")` |
| Total hours | `=SUMIFS(J:J,B:B,45)` |
| Hourly revenue | `=SUMIFS(L:L,B:B,45)` |
| Hours for one client | `=SUMIFS(J:J,B:B,45,C:C,"Harbor Bakery")` |

Copy these numbers into a new row of `weekly-summary.csv` during your Friday review.

## 5. Summary formulas
In `weekly-summary.csv`, with your columns in the order provided:

- **Utilisation %** = (billable + fixed-price hours) / total hours x 100
  `=ROUND((C2+D2)/F2*100,1)`
- **Effective rate** = all revenue earned / total hours worked (including admin)
  `=ROUND((H2+I2)/F2,2)`

"Fixed-price revenue earned" is the share of a fixed fee you've earned this week. A simple, honest way to estimate it: fixed price x the share of the project you completed this week. In the sample, Sam finished about 25% of a $2,800 website, so $700.

## 6. Project budget tracker
In `project-budget-tracker.csv`:

- **Budgeted hours** = fixed price / target hourly rate (rounded)
  `=ROUND(C2/D2,1)`
- **Hours used** = total of that project's rows in the timesheet
  `=SUMIFS(Timesheet!J:J,Timesheet!D:D,B2)`
- **Hours left** `=E2-F2`
- **% used** `=ROUND(F2/E2*100,1)`
- **% of work done** - your honest estimate, typed in by hand.
- **Status** `=IF(H2>I2+10,"Over",IF(H2>I2,"Watch","On track"))`

The status turns to **Watch** when you've used more of the hours than you've finished of the work, and **Over** when the gap is more than 10 points. That's your cue to check scope (see `weekly-review.md`).

## 7. Optional: one tab per year
When the sheet passes a few thousand rows, start a new tab for the new year and keep the old one for reference. Your formulas will stay fast.
files.logging-habits.md:
# Logging habits that stick

Time tracking only works if you actually do it. The goal is a log that's accurate to the quarter hour and takes less than five minutes a day.

## Pick one of three methods

**1. Live logging (most accurate).** Keep the timesheet open in a pinned tab. When you switch tasks, type the end time on the row you're finishing and start a new row. Best if you bill hourly and clients ask for detail.

**2. Notepad and end-of-day transfer (easiest to start).** Keep a scrap of paper or a plain note next to you. Each time you switch tasks, jot the time and a few words: `10:30 bakery print files`. At the end of the day, spend three minutes moving it into the sheet.

**3. Calendar blocking (best if your day is planned).** Plan your day as blocks in your calendar. At the end of the day, adjust the blocks to what really happened and copy them into the sheet. Good for people who already live in their calendar.

Whichever you pick, try it for two full weeks before changing. Most people give up in the first three days because they're trying to be perfect.

## Rounding rules
Decide once and write it down so your invoices are consistent:

- **Quarter hour (0.25)** - the most common choice and easy to explain.
- **Six minutes (0.1)** - common among consultants who bill large clients.
- **Round each block, not the day.** A 40-minute call is 0.75 hours, logged on its own row.
- **Be fair.** If you round, round to the nearest increment, not always up. Clients notice a pattern of 0.25-hour emails.

## Categories
Use a short, fixed list so your weekly totals mean something. Suggested:

| Category | Includes |
|---|---|
| Design / Writing / Development | The actual craft work (rename to fit your trade) |
| Meetings | Calls, video meetings, workshops |
| Production | File prep, uploads, handoffs, formatting |
| Admin | Invoicing, email triage, bookkeeping, scheduling |
| Sales | Proposals, discovery calls, follow-ups with leads |
| Marketing | Portfolio, social posts, newsletter |
| Learning | Courses, practice, research not tied to a client |

Keep it under ten. If you're inventing a new category every week, the list is too detailed.

## What counts as billable?
Agree this with each client and note it in your contract or proposal. Typical choices:

- **Usually billable:** project work, client meetings, revisions, research for that client, project-specific email.
- **Often billable but say so up front:** travel time, quick calls, small "can you just" requests.
- **Usually not billable:** proposals, invoicing, your own admin, fixing your own mistakes.

## Habits that help
- **Log the small stuff.** Ten 5-minute client emails a day is almost an hour. Log them as one row at the end of the day: `Client email (misc)`.
- **Write task names a client could read.** "Homepage revisions - round 1" beats "fixing stuff". You'll paste these straight into invoices.
- **Note scope changes as they happen.** If a client asks for something new on a call, put it in the notes column that day. It's your evidence later.
- **Don't track breaks.** Lunch, coffee and walking the dog are not rows. Only log work.
- **Fill gaps the same day.** Memory is good for about 24 hours. After that you're guessing.
files.weekly-review.md:
# Weekly review (15 minutes, every Friday)

Set a recurring calendar reminder. Do this before you close the laptop for the weekend.

## Part 1: Tidy the log (5 minutes)
- [ ] Every working day this week has rows. Fill any gaps from your calendar, sent emails and file history.
- [ ] Every row has a client, project, category and billable status.
- [ ] Client and project names are spelled consistently (so totals add up).
- [ ] Anything a client asked for that wasn't in the original scope is noted.

## Part 2: Fill in the weekly summary (5 minutes)
Add one row to `weekly-summary.csv` using the totals from `setup-guide.md`:

- [ ] Billable hours
- [ ] Fixed-price hours
- [ ] Non-billable hours
- [ ] Total hours
- [ ] Utilisation %
- [ ] Hourly revenue and fixed-price revenue earned
- [ ] Effective rate
- [ ] Update hours used in `project-budget-tracker.csv`

## Part 3: Read the numbers (5 minutes)
Answer these in a sentence each. Write the most important answer in the `top_time_sink` and `one_change_next_week` columns.

1. **Is my effective rate below my target rate?** If so, which client or project pulled it down?
2. **Is any fixed-price project marked Watch or Over?** If yes, is it because of scope creep (they asked for more) or estimation (it was harder than you thought)? Scope creep needs a conversation; estimation needs a higher quote next time.
3. **How much time went to admin?** If admin is more than about 15% of your week, what could you batch, template or drop?
4. **Did any one client take more time than they pay for?** Compare each client's share of your hours to their share of your income.
5. **What's the one change for next week?** Just one. Write it down.

## Reading the sample week
Sam's week 45:

- Total hours: 25.25. Billable 10.25, fixed-price 11, non-billable 4.
- Utilisation: 84%. Healthy; most of the week was client work.
- Effective rate: $52.08, below the $60 target. Why? The fixed-price website (Northside Physio) has used 51% of its budgeted hours for about 45% of the work.
- The client asked for an extra booking page on Wednesday's call. That's scope creep, not a slow designer.
- **One change:** send a short change request quoting the booking page separately before doing any work on it.

That one decision protects more money than any amount of working faster.

## Monthly add-on (first Friday of the month)
- [ ] Total last month's billable hours per client and create invoices (see `timesheet-to-invoice.md`).
- [ ] Compare your average effective rate this month to last month.
- [ ] Note your average weekly total hours. Is it sustainable for you?
files.timesheet-to-invoice.md:
# From timesheet to invoice

Clients pay faster when an invoice is clear, matches what they expected, and doesn't invite questions. Your timesheet already has everything you need.

## Step 1: Filter
Filter the timesheet to one client, one billing period and `billable = yes`. In Google Sheets or Excel: Data > Create a filter, then filter by client, date and billable.

## Step 2: Group into invoice lines
Don't paste 40 rows onto an invoice. Group by project and type of work. Most clients want 3-8 lines.

Use a pivot table (Insert > Pivot table) with:
- Rows: project, then task (or category)
- Values: SUM of hours, SUM of amount

## Step 3: Write lines a client recognises
Use the client's words for the work, not your internal shorthand.

| Weak line | Clear line |
|---|---|
| Design work - 8.25 h | Spring menu: layouts, final artwork and print files - 5.75 h |
| Misc | Client call to review menu layouts (2 Nov) - 0.5 h |
| Templates | Instagram template set incl. one round of revisions - 4 h |

## Step 4: Check before you send
- [ ] Hours on the invoice match the filtered timesheet total.
- [ ] Rate matches the agreed rate in the contract or proposal.
- [ ] Any extra work beyond the original scope was approved (email or message) and is labelled as such.
- [ ] Dates of the billing period are shown.
- [ ] Payment terms and due date are on the invoice.
- [ ] You've kept the timesheet extract in case the client asks for detail.

## Worked example
Sam's billable rows for Harbor Bakery, week 45:

| Project | Task | Hours | Amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spring menu design | Draft menu layouts | 2.5 | $150.00 |
| Spring menu design | Client call re: layouts | 0.5 | $30.00 |
| Spring menu design | Final menu artwork | 2.5 | $150.00 |
| Spring menu design | Print file prep | 0.75 | $45.00 |
| Social templates | Instagram template set | 3 | $180.00 |
| Social templates | Template revisions | 1 | $60.00 |
| **Total** | | **10.25** | **$615.00** |

Grouped into invoice lines:

```
INVOICE - Harbor Bakery
Billing period: 2-6 November 2026
Rate: $60/hour

1. Spring menu design - layout options, client review call,
   final artwork and print-ready files            6.25 h   $375.00
2. Social media templates - Instagram template set
   and one round of revisions (approved 5 Nov)    4.00 h   $240.00

Total                                            10.25 h   $615.00
Payment due within 14 days.
```

Two lines, every hour accounted for, and the new mini-project labelled with the date it was approved.

## Fixed-price projects
For fixed-price work, the invoice shows the agreed fee or milestone, not hours. Still log the hours: they tell you whether the price was right, and they're your evidence if you need to quote for extra work. In the sample, the Northside Physio invoice would show the milestone ("Website design - 50% on approval of designs: $1,400"), and the extra booking page would be a separate quote.

## If a client asks for the detail
Send the filtered timesheet extract (date, task, hours). Leave out internal notes. Having it ready, and offering it without fuss, builds a lot of trust.
